title: The Tribes Beyond the Jordan: Victory and Exile
summary: The chapter traces the tribes that settled east of the Jordan River: Reuben, whose birthright passed to Joseph, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. It records their victory over the Hagrites when they cried out to God and trusted him, and then their exile to Assyria after they were unfaithful and turned to the gods of the land.
story: Having dealt with the southern tribes of Judah and Simeon, the Chronicler crosses the Jordan to the east. Reuben was Jacob's firstborn and would normally come first, so the chapter begins by explaining why he doesn't: the birthright went to Joseph, and leadership came through Judah. The chapter then tells two short stories that frame the history of these eastern tribes. In the first, they cry out to God in battle and he answers because they trusted him. In the second, they break faith with God, and he stirs up the king of Assyria to carry them away. These two stories set out in miniature the pattern that will govern the whole book: seeking God brings help, and unfaithfulness brings exile.
historical:
Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh settled in the high plateau and pasture lands east of the Jordan after Moses defeated the kings Sihon and Og (Numbers 32; Deuteronomy 3). Their territory ran from the region north of the Arnon River in the south through Gilead to Bashan and Mount Hermon in the north. Several towns named here, including Aroer, Nebo, and Baal-meon (verse 8), also appear on the Moabite Stone, an inscription from about 840 BC set up by Mesha king of Moab, which describes his fighting with Israel in this very region and mentions that the men of Gad had lived in Ataroth from of old. The eastern tribes lived on a frontier, exposed to Moab, Aram, and the desert peoples.

Verse 17 dates a registration of Gad to the reigns of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, in the eighth century BC. Verses 6 and 26 name Tiglath-pileser III, king of Assyria from about 745 to 727 BC, who is also called Pul (a name he used as king of Babylon). Second Kings 15:29 records his campaign around 733 to 732 BC, when he took Gilead and Galilee and deported their people. The places of exile in verse 26, Halah, Habor, and the river of Gozan, lay in upper Mesopotamia and are also named in 2 Kings 17:6 and 18:11 for the deportations after Samaria fell in 722 BC.
cultural:
The birthright was the privilege of the firstborn son, usually a double share of the inheritance and the leadership of the family (Deuteronomy 21:17). Reuben lost it because he slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22; 49:3-4), an act that was not only sexual sin but a bid to claim his father's place. Jacob gave the double portion to Joseph by adopting his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own (Genesis 48). The Chronicler notes that leadership, though, came from Judah (verse 2). Honor and inheritance could be separated.

The eastern tribes lived largely by herding, and their wealth was counted in livestock: camels, sheep, and donkeys (verse 21). The Hagrites (named also in Psalm 83:6) were a nomadic people of the Syrian desert, and Jetur and Naphish are listed among the sons of Ishmael in 1 Chronicles 1:31, which suggests desert tribes related to the Ishmaelites. The language of prostitution in verse 25 is the prophets' common image for idolatry: Israel was bound to the LORD as a wife to a husband, and worshiping other gods was unfaithfulness to that marriage.
literary: The chapter has three genealogical sections (Reuben in verses 1 to 10, Gad in 11 to 17, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in 23 and 24), with two narrative sections set between and after them. The first narrative (verses 18 to 22) and the last (verses 25 and 26) mirror each other: in one the tribes trust God and he gives them the land of their enemies; in the other they are unfaithful and he gives them to their enemies. Both use the Chronicler's characteristic vocabulary: they cried out, they trusted, God answered, the battle belonged to God; and on the other side, they were unfaithful, and God stirred up the spirit of a foreign king. That last phrase will return at the very end of Chronicles, where the LORD stirs up the spirit of Cyrus to send the exiles home (2 Chronicles 36:22).

outline.t: Why Reuben the firstborn lost the birthright
The descendants of Reuben and their lands
The descendants of Gad in Bashan and Gilead
Victory over the Hagrites through trust in God

doctrines.note: Verse 20 gives the reason for victory plainly: they cried out to God in battle, and he answered them because they put their trust in him. The Chronicler presents trust in God, not military strength, as what decides the outcome.

The same tribes that trusted God later turned to the gods of the peoples whom God had destroyed before them. The chapter shows how quickly a people who have known God's help can drift into worshiping what he has already defeated.
God stirs up the spirit of the king of Assyria to carry out his judgment. Even a foreign emperor acting for his own ends serves God's purposes, a truth the book will return to with Cyrus.

words.note: Bekorah, birthright, the rights of the firstborn. Verses 1 and 2 separate the birthright (given to Joseph) from leadership (which came through Judah). The Chronicler explains the order of the tribes and why Judah and David stand at the center of his history.

Batach, to trust, to rely on someone for safety. It is the word of the Psalms for putting confidence in God rather than in horses, chariots, or princes. Here it is the reason God answered the eastern tribes in battle.

Maal, to act unfaithfully. The word returns in verse 25 to explain the exile of the eastern tribes. It describes a breach of trust, betraying a relationship of loyalty, and is the Chronicler's main word for the sin that leads to disaster.

Ur, to rouse or stir up. God stirs up the spirit of Tiglath-pileser to bring judgment. At the end of 2 Chronicles the same verb describes God stirring up Cyrus to end the exile. The God who sends his people away is the one who brings them back.

christ: The chapter's two stories set out the choice every generation of God's people faces: trust in God, or unfaithfulness to him. Israel's history showed that the people could not keep faith on their own for long. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one faithful son of Israel, who trusted his Father completely even in the battle of the cross, and whose faithfulness is counted for those who trust in him. The chapter also looks forward in another way. Tribes that were scattered to Assyria and never returned as tribes seemed lost to Israel for good. Yet the prophets spoke of God gathering all the scattered people of Israel, and the New Testament sees that hope beginning in Christ, who came to gather the lost sheep of Israel and people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16). That is a thematic connection, not a prediction in this chapter.

hard.q: Are the huge numbers of warriors, animals, and captives in this chapter meant literally?
hard.a: Verse 18 gives 44,760 warriors, and verse 21 lists 50,000 camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 captives. Numbers like these appear throughout the historical books, and interpreters handle them in different ways. Some take them as exact counts. Others note that the Hebrew word usually translated thousand (eleph) can also mean a clan or a military unit, so that some large totals may originally have counted units rather than individuals; this view is often applied to the census lists in Numbers and to Chronicles. Still others think some numbers were rounded or enlarged in the tradition to express the scale of God's victory. Each view has defenders among scholars who take Scripture seriously. The chapter's point doesn't depend on settling the question: the eastern tribes won a great victory because God helped them, and later lost everything because they left him.

questions: Reuben's one act of betrayal cost him the birthright. Why do some sins have consequences that last long after they are forgiven?
The same tribes who trusted God in battle later worshiped the gods of the land. What helps a person or a church keep faith after a season of answered prayer?

God used an Assyrian king to discipline his people and later a Persian king to bring them home. How does it change your view of world events to believe God is at work through rulers who don't know him?
